paragraphs: Friend, this passage is not a feel-good one, and I'm not going to dress it up. The Teacher looks at the place of judgment and sees "wickedness." He looks at the oppressed and sees "tears," and he says there was "no comforter" (Ecclesiastes 4:1). The lesson is that the Bible tells the truth about a broken world, and it lets you say the hard thing out loud.

But the Teacher doesn't stop at the pain. Right in the middle of it, he says in his heart, "God will judge the righteous and the wicked" (Ecclesiastes 3:17). He also looks at death and sees that men and beasts "all come from dust, and all return to dust" (Ecclesiastes 3:20), so he admits what he can't see: "Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward…" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). I love that, because he holds on to what he knows about God and doesn't fake an answer for the rest.

So what do you do with that, baker? When the unfair stuff piles up, you don't have to pretend it's fine, and you don't have to give up either. The Teacher says there is nothing better than to enjoy your work (Ecclesiastes 3:22), so you can do your good work today and leave the judging to God. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer feeling forgotten, and I can tell you this: a hard season is not the whole story, and God is still the One who sees.
